event: Christians are the largest, most widespread non-Muslim minority in Ottoman Palestine — bigger than the Jews. Gaza's Christians are ~25% of the city (the largest single minority community anywhere); Jerusalem's surpass the Jews by 1553-4. A rooted, multi-town population, three centuries before any great-power patron.
The Franciscan Custody of the Holy Land is established — the enduring Latin institutional anchor in Palestine.

The French Capitulations make France the recognized protector of Catholics across the Ottoman lands — the oldest of the great-power patronage links, and the lever Christians had that Jews and Samaritans did not.
Christians live under the same dhimmi extraction as the Jews — jizya, sumptuary distinction — overlaid with the chronic Holy-Places Status Quo disputes between the Greek-Orthodox and Latin clergy.
In the peasant revolt against Ibrahim Pasha, Bethlehem's Muslim quarter is destroyed and the Christians are caught in the upheaval — the shared pre-Tanzimat exposure to state-collapse violence.

On the Egyptian withdrawal an anti-Christian reaction runs 'throughout the country.' The Damascus Affair blood libel is instigated by Capuchin friars and the French consul — NOT by Muslims — and is repudiated by the returning Ottoman state (Abdülmecid's firman: 'the Hebrew nation will be protected'). The European blood-libel repertoire entered the Levant largely through Latin Christians.

The Anglo-Prussian Protestant bishopric of Jerusalem is founded — built explicitly as a counterweight to the 'feared expansion' of Russian and French influence. A tiny convert base, an outsized school footprint.

A French consul (1843) and a revived Latin patriarch (Joseph Valerga, 1847) re-establish the Latin presence under 'the apostolic mission of France, that most Catholic of nations' — the patriarchate abandoned since the Crusades.
17,800 Christians in the central+southern pachalik — versus 13,600 Jews. The second-largest community in the land, ahead of the Jews.

The Russian Ecclesiastical Mission (Bishop Porfiri Uspenski) begins — Orthodox great-power patronage of the Arab-Orthodox majority, though mediated (and partly captured) by the foreign Greek hierarchy of the Patriarchate.

The Status Quo firman freezes Holy-Places arrangements; the Orthodox-vs-Latin dispute over the church keys feeds directly into the Crimean War (1853-56). No other dhimmi community's situation was a casus belli among the great powers.

Hatt-i Hümayun proclaimed at the Seraglio in Jerusalem: all Ottoman subjects equal regardless of religion; churchbuilding eased; foreigners may own land. Finn: 'eminently distasteful to the old Mohammedan population.'

The great anti-Christian massacres — centered in Damascus and Mount Lebanon, NOT Palestine proper, though panic reigned among the Christians of Galilee. The flip side of the great-power-proxy prestige: the same patronage that drove Christian growth made them targets.

~41,952 Christians, about 11% of all Palestine — the fastest-growing community through the late Tanzimat. Ma'oz: 'the dramatic improvement was for Christians, who had European consular advocacy from France, Russia, and Britain.'

The Imperial Orthodox Palestine Society is founded; by 1914 it runs 101 schools / 10,400 pupils, 8 pilgrim hostels (cap. 10,000), a hospital and 6 clinics — the high-water mark of state patronage. Yet the Greek hierarchy blocked much of its reach to the Arab laity ('all attempts to found schools in Judea were in vain').

A church / monastery / school / hospital building boom transforms Jerusalem (the Russian Compound, the new-city institutions) — the soft-power, intelligentsia-forming face of the metropole that the Old Yishuv's halukah never produced.

The Arab-Orthodox laity's long struggle to wrest the Patriarchate from the foreign Greek hierarchy ('Arabization' — Arab-vs-foreign, lay-vs-clerical, Arabic-vs-Greek) trains an organized, literate lay cadre: the incubator of a secular Arab nationalism, before Palestinian nationalism had a name.

Najib Nassar (Greek-Orthodox milieu) founds al-Karmil — the first sustained Arabic-language anti-Zionist press organ. The man drawn to journalism 'to fight for the Arab Orthodox cause against the Greek clergy' turns the same energy on Zionism.

Issa al-Issa (Greek Orthodox) co-founds Filastin; Najib Nassar publishes al-Ṣihyūniyya, the first stand-alone Arabic anti-Zionist monograph. By 1913 Filastin prints al-Shaʿb al-Filastini — 'the Palestinian people.' The anti-Zionism is secular-nationalist in register, not theological.

Arab Orthodox leaders recast the church-Arabization movement as 'a political cause tied to Palestinian nationalism'; Filastin lends it 'a specifically nationalist orientation' — driven also, defensively, by the Mandate state's sectarian neglect of Palestinian Christians. (Sakakini and Antonius opposed the politicization.)
The Mandate censuses count ~71,000 (1922) → ~91,000 (1931) Christians — continued growth into the British period; the rooted community kept rising.
